Nekoda
neh-KOH-duh
proper noun
Hebrew Neqoda (H5353), marked or distinguished — from naqod (H5348), speckled, marked with spots; the word used of Jacob's speckled flocks.

Biblical Definition

Nekoda names two groups in the registers of the return, and the second is the striking one. A family of Nekoda stands among the Nethinim, the temple servants (Ezr 2:48; Neh 7:50). But another company of the children of Nekoda appears in a different and poignant list: those who went up from Telmelah… but they could not shew their father's house, and their seed, whether they were of Israel (Ezr 2:59-60; Neh 7:61-62). They came home with everyone else, six hundred and fifty-two of them, and could not prove they belonged. The registers do not expel them and do not confirm them; they write the fact down and leave it standing. In the parallel case of the priests who could not find their register, the ruling was that they were put from the priesthood till there stood up a priest with Urim and with Thummim (Ezr 2:63) — office suspended, the question referred to God. The name means marked, from the word for speckled flocks, and there is a quiet irony in it: a house called marked that could not produce its mark.

Origin & Era

A name in the registers of the return: a family of the Nethinim, and a company who could not prove their Israelite descent.

NEKODA, Hebrew Neqoda, marked, distinguished; from the word for speckled.

1. The head of a family of the Nethinim, the servants of the temple.

2. The head of a company who returned but could not shew their father's house.

Six hundred fifty and two came up who could not prove their seed, whether they were of Israel.

The priests in the same case were put from the priesthood until a priest should stand up with Urim and Thummim.

Key Scripture

Ezr 2:48 — "The children of Rezin, the children of Nekoda, the children of Gazzam,"

Ezr 2:60 — "The children of Delaiah, the children of Tobiah, the children of Nekoda, six hundred fifty and two."

Neh 7:50 — "The children of Reaiah, the children of Rezin, the children of Nekoda,"

Neh 7:62 — "The children of Delaiah, the children of Tobiah, the children of Nekoda, six hundred forty and two."

Modern Corruption

Assurance is grounded in feeling or in mere profession; Scripture grounds it in evidence God Himself supplies, and is honest when the evidence is missing.

expand to see more

The children of Nekoda who could not shew their father's house are a standing rebuke to two opposite errors about assurance. The first is presumption — the assumption that anyone who walks in with the crowd belongs, that a profession made once settles the matter and no evidence need ever appear. The registers of Ezra and Nehemiah were kept precisely because Israel did not think that. Belonging was a matter of fact, and facts can be checked.

The second error is the despair that says no one can know. Scripture insists that assurance is available and commends the pursuit of it: These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life (1Jn 5:13), and give diligence to make your calling and election sure (2Pe 1:10). But the evidence is of a particular kind — the Spirit bearing witness with our spirit (Rom 8:16), and a changed life: we know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren (1Jn 3:14). The honest handling in Ezra 2, which neither expelled the doubtful nor pretended the question was settled, is the pastoral model: tell the truth about what is unproved, and refer the case to the Priest who is able to settle it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Neqoda (H5353), from naqod (H5348), speckled, marked with spots.

expand to see more

Hebrew naqod (H5348) — speckled, marked; used of Jacob's flocks in Genesis 30-31.

Hebrew Neqoda (H5353) — a family of the Nethinim and a company of uncertain descent, Ezra 2:48, 2:60, Nehemiah 7:50, 7:62.

Hebrew yachas (H3187) — to reckon by genealogy, to enrol; the verb of the registers.

Hebrew Urim (H224) and Thummim (H8550) — lights and perfections; the means by which doubtful cases were referred to God.

Greek plerophoria (G4136) — full assurance; the full assurance of hope unto the end (Heb 6:11).

Usage

"“The children of Rezin, the children of Nekoda, the children of Gazzam” — among the Nethinim."

"“They could not shew their father's house… whether they were of Israel” (Ezr 2:59)."

"“Till there stood up a priest with Urim and with Thummim” (Ezr 2:63)."
